maintopic: STATEMENT ON FEED GRAIN SITUATION IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: STATEMENT ON FEED GRAIN SITUATION IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a statement with regard to the feed grain situation in the prairie provinces. The Canadian wheat board has been keeping in close touch with the development of the 1958 grain crop in the prairie provinces, and particularly with the drought disaster which has struck such wide areas of Manitoba and Saskatchewan. It is now apparent that great loss has been sustained and, as time goes on, the possibility of recovery is becoming more limited.
The wheat board has completed a survey of deliverable stocks of wheat, oats and barley on farms at all the 2,100 delivery points in the prairie provinces. Fortunately there are substantial reserve stocks of feed grains on farms in all three western provinces and, although all these stocks are not evenly distributed, they do constitute an important measure of security in conditions which now prevail.
Over and above farm stocks of feed grain there are over 50 million bushels of oats and barley in country elevators at this date. Part of these stocks can be mobilized to meet acute feed and seed problems as they arise. In spite of the widespread drought there are ample supplies of feed grain in the prairie provinces, although these stocks are not necessarily within the area where they may ultimately be required.
As a first step in meeting the problem which has arisen, the wheat board is prepared to hold in country elevators such supplies of wheat, oats and barley as the provincial and municipal authorities think advisable.
In carrying out this policy of retention the wheat board will follow policies pursued some years ago. Provincial and municipal authorities will arrange with elevator companies for the retention of needed stocks of these grains and will provide that the necessary carrying charges are taken care of. An instruction has been issued today by the wheat board setting forth the method which may be followed by the provincial and municipal authorities and the elevator companies.
At the present time the wheat board has quite large sales commitments, but the board will be in a position to play its part in relieving any distress that may result from the present adverse crop conditions in some parts of Saskatchewan and Manitoba.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON FEED GRAIN SITUATION IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the announcement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce is most timely, and I believe it is a measure of insurance which ought to be taken at this time. We hope that crop conditions will improve; we have seen prairie conditions improve very rapidly, and we hope that this planned step may not be necessary in the final analysis.
I wonder if the minister or his department or the government have considered whether the transfer of the grain that may be involved from places where it is now in store to some other places where it may be needed may be done on the basis of the Crowsnest pass freight rates, the low freight rates, rather than the very high freight rates on smaller movements of grain. I think that is an important consideration.

maintopic: STATEMENT ON FEED GRAIN SITUATION IN PRAIRIE PROVINCES
speechtext: I will look into that. I have not received from the wheat board the instructions they are issuing today to the provincial authorities and the elevator companies, and in those instructions perhaps that point is mentioned.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, July 2, consideration of the motion of Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I should like to compliment the Minister of Finance on a very creditable oratorical effort and on the few changes made on government revenue which were welcomed nevertheless. In this budget one or two items are noticeably conspicuous by their absence and I wish to comment on them. One in particular was not even mentioned, notwithstanding every expectation that it would be dealt with in the government's first budget. I am referring to the excise tax on automobiles, against which the minister spoke long and loudly when in opposition. According to the record he waxed eloquently against this tax. I quote from the May 3, 1955, budget debate speech in which the then hon. member as reported at page 3395, said this about the tax:
The excise tax has largely been ignored in the minister's approach to the problem-
Oh, they made much of the removal of the luxury tax-because that is the guise in which it was introduced a few years ago-on tires for motor vehicles. They have made much of the reduction of the excise tax from 15 per cent to 10 per cent on motor vehicles. Well, what they have done, in the way they have gone about it-in leaving the tax at far too high a figure, and giving no benefit at all to those dealers who had a stocked-up inventory of motor cars-has been to bedevil the wholesale and retail motor car business in Canada today.
Then again in volume 3 of Hansard of 1956, on March 27, 1956, the minister as reported at page 2648, had this to say:
The second feature of the sales and excise taxes which is worthy of mention relates to a reduction that was made last year. The government last year actually reduced from 15 to 10 per cent the excise tax levied on automobiles. What was the result, sir? A reduction in revenue? On the contrary, there was an increase in revenue. The collections from the excise tax on automobiles actually exceeded those of the previous year by $8 million. I suggest that there is a lesson there to be learned by the Minister of Finance and by the government. A few more reductions in rate would not necessarily mean serious and crippling reductions in revenues. On the contrary they would assist the circulation of money and the expansion of business enterprise.
Evidently he no longer believes in his own statement. Then again the Prime Minister, speaking on January 14, 1955, as reported at page 192 of Hansard, had this to say:
What are we doing to meet the situation? What is the reason tor it? We have said that over the years Canadians were being taxed out of the markets of the world and taxed out of their jobs. I know they used to say you could make jobs without profits. We have learned differently In Saskatchewan with the disappearance of the mirage of 1944.
What about hidden taxes? The average automobile has a hidden tax of $400. This government in its wisdom has decreed a high cost structure in the last few years. It has isolated our trade. It has started the march of unemployment. I believe
The Budget-Mr. Badanai
that Canada's industry must be revitalized by giving tax relief at once. The government must act and act now.
That is precisely what the members of Her Majesty's loyal opposition are now saying, and that is what we are standing for.
During the last session of parliament the minister reduced the tax by 2J per cent. The reduction was made without giving an account of government spending plans, but we were encouraged to believe that in the very first budget, which the people were expecting before the election of March 31, this tax would at long last be consigned to the limbo where all existing government inequities were to be purged.
This tax was conceived as luxury tax when only a few people could afford to own and operate a car. Then the war came along and an all-out struggle demanded the curtailment of civilian spending and all available money had to be channeled into war loans. The automobile industry needs a stimulant rather than a deterrent. The excise tax today is a factor in lowering the sales of automobiles in this country where they are a vital necessity. This was pointed out by the hon. member for Middlesex East when he spoke during the budget debate on March 19, 1957, as recorded at page 2492 of Hansard, as follows:
There is no doubt the day is coming when some arrangements will have to be made whereby the municipalities and the provinces will have a greater share of the tax dollar. Their necessities are still taxed . . . Probably the motorist is the most heavily taxed individual in this country, yet an automobile is a necessity in our country of vast distances and for transportation to employment.
I say amen to that. In many cases the automobile is actually a tool of production. Over 80 per cent of all cars driven in Canada are driven in the pursuit of business. We do not place an excise tax on the carpenter's saw or the plumber's wrench, but we do place an excise tax on automobiles which are equally used as tools to enable people to earn a living. It is no easier for a salesman to earn a living-and believe me, I can speak from actual experience-than it is for a carpenter to do so. To place an excise tax on the automobile is therefore a deterrent to the sale of cars, as has been amply demonstrated many times when there has been a rumour of a tax cut.
You might recall that last December when a Toronto newspaper printed such a report on November 28, 1957 under the banner headline, "Ottawa to Cut Car Excise Tax" the government was not in a position to comment upon it. There was no reliable estimate of a probable budget, as has been the case in previous years, and people who wished to buy cars cancelled orders placed with dealers in order to see what saving they might enjoy if the tax were removed.

The Budget-Mr. Badanai Naturally the automobile dealers across the country sought immediate action, and meantime automobile companies closed down because they could not sell their cars. General Motors closed down for two days, Chrysler for four days and Ford of Canada laid off some 2,400 people a few days prior to the appearance of the headline I have quoted. This meant that thousands upon thousands of Canadian workingmen were laid off and deprived of income with consequent suffering to their families and communities. This is just one indication of public awareness of the excise tax on automobiles and the money which this tax costs the public.
If the public suspects the excise tax on cars might be removed the sales of cars stop, and I submit that the very presence of this 7J per cent tax on passenger cars is a threat to the steady employment of thousands of Canadians. I am convinced that its removal would provide more jobs and more steady employment than any measure the government has so far introduced in an effort to reduce unemployment. This is a serious handicap to have hanging over an industry so vital to the economic well-being of Canada. The excise tax creates instability in this major industry upon which so many people from coast to coast are entirely dependent for their livelihood.
I wonder if hon. members realize that one in every seven persons in the entire labour force of Canada is employed in the automobile industry, exclusive of service stations dispensing products necessary for the operation of motor vehicles. In other words this tax creates a situation of instability for this large group of Canadians.
Automobiles are taxed in so many ways on both a federal and provincial basis that it would require a lengthy computation by a battery of so-called mechanical brains to find out just how much of the cost of a car is accounted for by taxes. Let me cite a few instances. The latest figure I can obtain is for 1956, when ten provinces in Canada collected $383,765,000, which was equal to 24.9 per cent of the total revenue of those ten provinces. In 1956 the federal government collected from the 10 per cent sales tax almost $98 million and from the 10 per cent excise tax $72,250,000. True, the excise tax- and it is about that tax I am speaking and not the sales tax-was reduced to 7J per cent last December. The sales tax of course remained at 10 per cent.
All these millions of dollars, plus special automobiles taxes in some of the provinces and in some municipalities, when placed on the purchase price of a car have a seriously deterrent effect on car sales. This is particularly important this year, when we should


be doing everything possible to stimulate and not to hold back business.
The removal of the 7J per cent excise tax on passenger cars, to my mind, would be the best way to stimulate employment. I can think of no better way to stimulate the economy, to provide more employment for the over 40,000 people working in the motor vehicle industry in Canada. To illustrate the importance of the industry I should like to quote the following figures. In the first five months of 1956 the industry paid out in wages a total of $70,263,588, while for the same period in 1957 the figure was $74,446,692. For the first five months of 1958 the figure was $63,361,036. These figures apply only to persons engaged in the manufacture of new motor vehicles in this country.
During the same five-month period in 1956 the government collected in sales tax $43,645,371 and in excise tax $34,679,323, a total of $78,324,692. In the same five-month period in 1957 the government collected in sales tax $49,941,684 and $39,681,983 in excise tax, a total of $89,623,667. And for the first five months of 1958, this calendar year, it collected in sales tax $39,401,540 and in excise tax $23,837,996, for a total of $63,239,536.
Now, Mr. Speaker, before proceeding further I would ask leave of the house to have this table incorporated in the proceedings of Hansard. It is a table showing revenues received by the federal government from 1914 to December, 1957.

But even these figures, impressive as they are, do not tell the whole story. Canadian automobile manufacturers are purchasing materials and parts from thousands of suppliers. I have only the figures of one company, General Motors of Canada. In 1957 this company purchased Canadian goods to the tune of $425 million and I assume the other Canadian car manufacturers are spending proportionate amounts with Canadian suppliers, which all adds up to the tremendous contribution of the automobile industry to the national economy.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in view of these facts I do not see how the government can ignore this awkward situation confronting one of the industries which is giving Canada so much, and contributing to the employment and welfare of so many. I respectfully suggest that the minister give assurance to this house that this matter of the excise tax on automobiles is not made final, and that he will give serious consideration in the near future to the complete elimination of this tax. There might have been justification for it at one time, but if there was any good reason for it in the past that justification is now obsolete and unwarranted.
There is another matter in which I am particularly interested, and that is the plight of our poor municipalities. If there was any expectation that the budget would contain some sign of assistance to the municipalities, with the exception of the removal of the sales tax on certain municipal purchases, for which we are grateful, with the announcement that the federal government will be offering large blocks of bonds to the public every few months these long-nursed hopes were shattered. These offerings will have a decided effect on limiting the amount of municipal debentures that may be offered, and also any that are offered will have to carry a high interest rate if they are to be sold in Canada.
This budget will force municipal governments to borrow in the United States. The failure to include in the budget a measure to establish a pool or a loan fund to which municipilities may sell their debentures at a reasonable rate of interest was, from the standpoint of the municipalities, a serious omission. Such a loan fund would be of inestimable assistance to the hard-pressed municipal governments. It seems to me to be the only system which would provide them with funds to continue with their progressive construction programs, and keep a goodly number of people employed.
Perhaps investment dealers or brokers do not look favourably upon such pool or loan fund for the obvious reason that, if established, such a fund would take away competitive marketing. I am not suggesting

that the government was influenced by financial institutions in its failure to giving serious consideration to this important and vital issue. I am pointing out, however, that the minister in his closing remarks said:
This budget has been born of confidence in Canada's future, not blind wishful thinking, but unshrinkable realism.
I for one fail to see the realism of the Minister of Finance when he overlooks the immense task of the municipalities of Canada, the oldest form of democratic government, the level of government closest to the people, which is the most responsive to the requirements and needs of Canadians. I cannot see much realism, I regret to say, in a budget which totally ignores an industry such as the automobile industry which has contributed billions to the wealth of the nation.
The fact that only one company purchased goods from more than 4,000 suppliers in more than 400 communities is proof that without a healthy and prosperous automobile industry Canada could not possibly expect much from the vision of development so eloquently portrayed by the Prime Minister and echoed by the Minister of Finance in his two-hour budget speech in the house on June 17. I express the hope that the government will see fit to give this industry another look, and I am confident that there would be no dissension in this house if finally once and for all this iniquitous excise tax were removed.
I was very happy to see the Minister of Labour here this afternoon. I am sorry he is absent at the moment, but I know he would support my contention. The minister and I worked closely together when he was mayor of the city of Oshawa. Coming as he does from a community which is practically wholly dependent upon the automotive industry I know he would also support this measure to eliminate the excise tax on automobiles. This measure would be received by the municipalities and the people of Canada as a beneficial and progressive one designed to achieve the very things this government has so eloquently advocated, not only while its members were in opposition but during the recent election campaign and also in the throne speech.
Here my case on behalf of the automotive industry and the municipalities of Canada rests.

Mr. Speaker, on talking with many of my constituents over the past week end I found that the majority were happy with the contents of this budget, and they had not been expecting miracles such as the opposition critics have intimated was their expectation. They felt that their confidence in this government had again been justified. For those who think in terms of all the people there is very little fault to be found with this budget. Never in the history of Canada were our citizens enjoying a better standard of living. Granted, we have problems and they will perhaps always be with us; nevertheless this government has faced present difficulties and adopted an earnest, sound approach to their solution.
The criticism directed at the government in respect of unemployment by two or three members of the opposition has become monotonous and nauseating. These hon. gentlemen have been instrumental in creating fear and aggravating this regrettable situation. Their propaganda in the last session as well as in this one has influenced 57071-3-118
The Budget-Mr. Noble many timid business people who have postponed making decisions which could have added much momentum to an upturn in business and employment. Some positive thinking and constructive suggestions would be more appreciated by the government and those who are inconvenienced by what is presently a weak link in our economy. However, in spite of these alarmists business and employment are on the upswing.
Mr. Speaker, with your indulgence I will quote a short editorial that I think is appropriate on this occasion. The editorial is entitled, "The Awful Uncertainty of the Future" and reads as follows:
It is a gloomy moment in history. Not in the lifetime of any man who reads his paper has there been so much grave and deep apprehension; never has the future seemed so dark and hard to calculate.
In France the political cauldron seethes and bubbles with uncertainty.
England and the British empire is being sorely tried and exhausted in a social and economic struggle, with turmoil at home and uprising of her teeming millions in her far-flung empire.
The United States is beset with racial, industrial and commercial chaos, drifting we know not where.
Russia hangs like a storm cloud on the horizon of Europe-dark, menacing and foreboding.
It is a solemn moment, and no man can feel indifference, which happily, no man pretends to feel in the issue of events.
Of our own troubles, no man can see the end.
This editorial sounds pretty gloomy, does it not? The writer evidently was weighed down by present problems and quite ready to sell himself and our nation short. Did I say present problems? Excuse me, please; far from it. This editorial appeared before world war II, before the depression of 1929, before the first world war in 1914, before the panic of 1891 and before the civil war in 1865. This was an editorial which appeared in Harper's magazine on October 10, 1847, well over 100 years ago. Yes, pessimism is the scarecrow that fear erects in the watermelon patch of the future to frighten away the timid souls so the feast may be richer for the few who are not afraid. We still have these gloom artists with us. As a matter of fact we have too many in the House of Commons, on the opposition benches, who would rate as experts in this profession.
At this point I would like to say the riding I have the honour to represent lies along the southwest shore of Georgian bay. It is made up of nine townships and five urban centres consisting of Owen Sound, Meaford, Thom-bury, Clarksburg and Shallow Lake. Although we have considerable industry, agriculture constitutes the largest share of my constituency's earning power. The people are basically Anglo-Saxon in origin. However, recent immigration has introduced some Dutch people into my riding. I am proud to say this
1866	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Noble adds up to a thrifty populace of sound citizens. I want to point out that the people of my constituency desire government recognition, but they realize that the first duty of the government is to attack problems of national importance, and I feel the Minister of Finance dealt fairly with one and all in the budget for this fiscal year.
Agricultural conditions in Grey North have improved during the past year. However, small operations in mixed farming have ceased to be economically sound and the trend is toward larger farms properly mechanized. Some farmers have improved their position through specialization, and it is quite evident this course will be followed by others. Our most successful farmers are those who have the latest scientific methods of operation. Soil is tested so that it may be properly treated for best results. Special attention is given to a program of herd improvement. The net result is more food produced by fewer people. By this progress a process of elimination is taking place. People without the capital and other qualifications necessary to participate in this type of farming are drifting into other phases of our economy where we hope they may be satisfactorily absorbed. However, it is gratifying to know that the Canadian Farm Loan Act stands to be amended. This could help those in need of capital, especially our young farmers.
One branch of our agricultural specialization that has been successful in my riding is the production of apples. In the Meaford-Thornbury area there are more than 3,000 acres of apple orchards. It is an accepted fact in the trade that some of the choicest apples on the continent are produced in this area. These apples are kept at their best for many months after harvesting by three large up to date cold storage plants.
In the past these people have experienced considerable difficulty marketing their crop in competition with United States growers. Perhaps some of the competition was fair; nevertheless when production was good across the line it was apparent that dumping contributed to some of the grief experienced by our growers. Because of this budget, with its promise of strict enforcement of the antidumping law, and with the hope that the Department of Agriculture will allow only the better grade of apples entrance to Canada, our growers may look to a future with brighter prospects.
I hesitate to speak about matters which concern me in a personal way, but since I bring to this house some experience in the field of fur breeding, and since this industry has not had a voice heretofore to explain its position, perhaps I might be excused for bringing to your attention, Mr. Speaker, some


of its highlights and problems. After all, many people in Canada are dependent on this industry for their livelihood. Shipments of fur to the United States and other countries have brought millions of dollars into our economy.
I am in the unique position of being the only member of this house representing the fur industry. Of course I fully realize that this industry does not play a major role in our economy. However, the fur trade influenced our early colonization and in those years was the wealth and the key industry of Canada. Through the years of early development wild fur was in plentiful supply, but during the following years of exploitation fur became scarce and this prompted the birth of a new, specialized branch of agriculture, namely that of fur ranching.
As its representative in Ottawa, Mr. Speaker, I will do my utmost to keep this house informed of its problems. Our relationship with the United States, Canada's best market, has been all that could be desired. We have co-operated fully with the United States ranchers in a program of continuous advertising, and the United States market has always been open to us. We in our industry trust that this spirit of neighbourliness may always exist, and that our Department of Trade and Commerce will continue to foster close co-operation and good will with our friends to the south.
Perhaps at this time you will allow me to take a few minutes to tell you something of the phenomenal development which has taken place in ranch mink during recent years. As most hon. members know, mink can now be produced in many shades of grey, blue and brown, also extra dark brown which is almost black and, of course, white. These are all natural colours known as mutations, and are not dyed or bleached. At our ranch we produced the first mutations in Canada, and we were the original breeders of white mink anywhere in the world.
In mink, as in all other livestock, we have disease problems. The two biggest killers have been distemper and virous enteritis. However, the spread of rabies across the country is cause for some concern. The former disease we have been able to control satisfactorily with a live virus vaccine but the latter has been causing serious losses for several years. Virus enteritis originated on a ranch in the neighbourhood of the Fort William garbage dump, thereby linking the disease with rats.
The budget gave encouragement to the extermination of this pest, which is costing our country millions of dollars annually as a disease carrier and a culprit of destruction. Since the time of the original outbreak

at Fort William thousands of mink have fallen victims of this disease. Much research has been done and many experiments have been carried on. The government laboratory at Hull did considerable work on the disease but gave up about three years ago. I pay tribute to the Ontario veterinary college for the contribution they are making in helping the mink producers protect their herds against this devastating disease. Within the next few weeks many mink will be vaccinated with a vaccine produced by this institution in the hope that some protection may be afforded those areas where the disease is known to exist.
This government supports an experimental fur farm at Summerside, Prince Edward Island, under the supervision of Dr. Gunn. I feel that this project has outlived its usefulness at this location. It served a purpose when Prince Edward Island was the centre of the silver fox industry, but since this phase of fur ranching is terribly neglected with very little hope of recovery I think it is time this institution was moved to Ontario, the heart of the mink industry in Canada. Today the mink industry is the fur industry. Our country is climatically ideal for fur production. The food used on fur farms is almost exclusively by-products which would be of little value otherwise.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I urge this government to encourage and foster this young industry, and to give careful consideration to the establishment of an up to date dominion experimental fur ranch in Ontario where it could work in close collaboration with the Hull laboratory and the Ontario veterinary college.
In Grey North, manufacturing is confined mostly to Owen Sound and Meaford, though Thornbury and Shallow Lake have some small plants with good growth possibilities. The two larger urban centres have several woodworking factories that produce flooring, windows and doors, furniture, radio and television cabinets and many other wood products. Owen Sound has two modern plants producing electrical products, also an up to date publishing company specializing in office stationery, bookbinding and other paper products. In Meaford we have a modern textile mill which at present is having a difficult time. However, all these manufacturers are pleased indeed with the assurance given in the budget that they will not have to compete with any dumped products, and that textiles will be given further consideration.
Owen Sound boasts of one of the most modern engineering works and steel, iron and bronze foundries in Canada. This plant
57071-3-118J
The Budget-Mr. Noble is capable of turning out castings which are calculated by the ton. They are equipped to build large propellers, and during the war this shop produced propellers for all the ships built in Canada. They have produced a new metal which is especially adapted for the construction of propellers for icebreakers and other boats which have constant contact with ice. I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that since this plant contributed so much in our time of need it should be given first consideration by the government in competition with propeller manufacturers outside this country.
My riding, located as it is on a fine body of water, has several boat manufacturers. From these establishments come some of the finest pleasure craft available anywhere. The largest of these plants is equipped to build steel barges, landing craft and boats up to 150 feet long, with a tonnage of up to 580 tons. Other steel products manufactured by this company are transformers, lighting poles, road rollers, marine gas and oil drilling equipment. With this line of products this firm will be in a position to make a notable contribution to the development of our north country.
There is an urgent desire by the people of my constituency for more industry. We must have more work if we are to absorb the growing labour force and supply a livelihood for the people who prefer to live in the ideal and pleasing surroundings of Grey North. I hope that decentralization will be given serious consideration, and that this government will use its influence in the encouragement of this plan. It is essential from the point of national security, and would work needed benefit in our smaller urban centres.
Industrial development corporations were instrumental in developing Toronto's golden mile of industry, but these corporations are reluctant to operate in smaller cities off the beaten path where the possibilities of profitable business for them are less favourable. However, Mr. Speaker, a group of public-spirited citizens in Owen Sound have banded themselves together and propose forming a company. Their purpose will be the raising of money through the sale of shares in this company. With the money they propose to render the same service to their city and community that is extended to the larger centres by the industrial development corporations; but to be successful considerable government help will be needed. Not forgetting decentralization, Mr. Speaker, I suggest this government make available, on long-term loan, an amount equal to that raised by any public organization for the purpose of industrial promotion.
The tourist industry has grown to be one of Canada's major industries. Grey North,

The Budget-Mr. Noble with Georgian bay as its northern boundary, shares handsomely in the dividends from this industry. Accommodation is available on sandy beaches or on rugged shore lines, and for those wishing to establish their own summer homes excellent building lots can be secured at reasonable prices. In this budget the tax exemption extended to building materials should give stimulation to summer cottage building.
At Owen Sound first-class passenger boat service is scheduled to points in the upper lakes for the duration of the tourist season. At Meaford pleasure craft with licensed guides are at the service of visitors for water tours or fishing trips. Meaford is visited by yachts from many points in the United States as well as in Canada, and is reputed to be the finest harbour on the great lakes for small craft. This harbour is in urgent need of floating docks, and I feel certain the Department of Public Works will remedy this matter.
I would be remiss in my duty if I did not mention the beautiful scenery in Grey North. It is unsurpassed in any part of Canada. With the welfare of the tourist industry in mind, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that we facilitate travel by United States citizens through our country. In this respect may I suggest the swift completion of a better means of travel between Canada and the United States at Sault Ste. Marie. This is a fine place to enter Canada, as a great area open to fishing and hunting is immediately available. Even more important to this point of entry was the completion of the famous Mackinac bridge which makes possible a flow of traffic 15 times greater than before. However, without a bridge at Sault Ste. Marie we have a serious bottleneck to the free flow of traffic into Canada.
I am informed that an act was passed by parliament on May 4, 1955, to incorporate the St. Mary's Bridge Company for the purpose of constructing and maintaining a toll bridge across the St. Mary's river at the Sault. The Canadian company was to enter into an agreement with the international bridge authority of Michigan to do this, and their agreement with that commission was approved by the governor in council on September 9, 1955.
No work was actually done on this venture. This first arrangement apparently broke down. Then the state of Michigan began negotiating with the province of Ontario, and this was the position as far as the federal government was concerned up to February 13, 1958. Subsequently, however, the two original companies have submitted a plan to the Department of Transport for a projected location of this structure. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker,

that after the delay of three years since parliament recognized the necessity for this bridge it is now urgent that some influence be directed by the government toward the early completion of this venture.
Plans for improved ferry service from South Bay to Tobermory are now being considered. This is a very popular tourist route, and with the improved facilities I have mentioned many thousands more Americans would visit Canada and a corresponding increase in their spending would result.
I am very well aware of the fact that the British North America Act gave the federal government legal jurisdiction over coastal and inland fisheries. However, by agreement the province of Ontario has taken over the management of fisheries within its boundaries. This arrangement worked very well over the years when Georgian bay and lake Huron, the areas in which I am particularly interested, were well stocked with lake trout and whitefish, but now that these waters have become almost depleted of these species our fishermen have fallen on evil days. These regrettable circumstances could have been contributed to by unsuitable legislation for the conservation of these fish or laws that were not enforced. Fishermen were allowed to go on the spawning beds and take fish, which has proven to be a serious mistake. At that very time these fish were having a tremendous struggle for survival. Lamprey eels were taking a terrific toll. The areas were being heavily populated with smelts. This fish if fed raw carries an enzyme that destroys the vitamin B in any given diet, with the result of paralysis and eventually death. I have proven this in mink feeding. I feel that smelts have also contributed to the disappearance of trout and whitefish.
The federal government has entered into a convention with the United States government in an effort to control the lamprey eel and to rehabilitate whitefish and lake trout in the great lakes. In Georgian bay, which is completely Canadian water, I suggest to the government that immediate stimulation be given a program of conservation and rehabilitation in co-operation with the provincial government. This body of water, which in the past produced millions of dollars of revenue through food and as a mecca for tourist fishermen, is now reduced to a good place for boating.
For example, a few seasons ago in the harbour at Meaford 35 fishing craft for the purpose of trolling for lake trout were kept completely occupied for several months each season. Each boat accommodated four passengers and a guide. I regret to inform

you, Mr. Speaker, that not one boat now leaves Meaford harbour to troll for lake trout. The chamber of commerce of Meaford estimates that the loss to the town is in excess of $250,000 annually. The people who are suffering more directly are the commercial fishermen who have thousands of dollars invested in tugs, nets, warehouses and other equipment. They are scattered up and down the shores of this largest fresh water bay on the continent.
In Grey county we are sharing in three conservation authorities. These are on the Saugeen, Sauble and Beaver rivers. The last mentioned is completely within the boundaries of Grey county. In the development of these authorities, and not forgetting the fact that we have large tracts of land not suitable for agriculture, an excellent opportunity is presented for the establishing of camp grounds and a national park. I realize that the provincial government is required to take the initiative in these projects before federal assistance can be expected. However, I want to commend this government for the keen interest and consideration they have extended with regard to this particular development. We in our riding plan to take advantage of this opportunity.
Considering our whole economy, I am satisfied that the finance minister has gone all out to correct the immediate problems on which the budget could work any remedy. At this time I want to repeat the wise words of the finance minister when he said, as found at page 1250 of Hansard of June 17:
Only by keeping our costs of production in line with those of our competitors can we hope to achieve expanding employment and progressive improvement in our standard of living.
The economic growth and recovery we desire to bring about must take the form, as pointed out by the Prime Minister not of higher costs and prices but more production and more jobs.

Mr. Speaker, there was naturally a somewhat marked disparity between the speech that introduced the budget and the speech the Minister of Finance made yesterday. We were back again yesterday to those lovely phrases such as "crocodile tears", "crystal clear", and "welter of contradictions", which I thought the minister had perhaps departed from forever with the relative dignity and, may I say, underplayed presentation given the budget. In his speech yesterday the minister proceeded to take everybody to task, and I suppose he should certainly be allowed that delight because of the fact that he has sat here and listened to so much.
The Budget-Mr. Fisher
He started off by saying that much of the criticism had been contradictory and none of it had been very constructive. Of course the charge that criticism is not constructive is really a red herring. It is not a logical answer. I think the fact that some of the criticism is contradictory is only to be expected when there are so many different interests in this country. For example, there are those who favour higher tariffs and those who favour lower tariffs.
But it seems to me that the contradictions are paralleled by the budget itself. I know I have felt, so far as some of the criticism the Liberal party has made of the government since assuming office is concerned, that much of it has been sour grapes. For example, with respect to dominion-provincial relations the Liberals managed to keep Quebec in a sort of post-Regina, scaffold trauma for many years, and it was certainly about time and most desirable that that hold be broken. I welcome the fact that the Bourbonnais and the Hardy Smalls, the Cathers and the Pigeons are lying down in the same political tent, and I think the Liberal party may be making too much of the disparities. Perhaps we will get something from this government in time. We may even see the Conservative party push some of the Quebec politicians into the twentieth century.
In that regard I think the Tremblay report makes very interesting reading. This is the report on constitutional problems published several years ago. It stresses constitutional and fiscal problems, and there are two paragraphs here that I think should be very much in the mind of the Minister of Finance if indeed they represent the point of view of Quebec as the commission suggests and if, to carry it a step further, these ideas represent the opinions of the members from Quebec who now form such a large part of the party in power. On page 22 of the summary of the report there is the following:
Since indirect taxes, within the meaning of constitutional jurisprudence, are assigned to the federal government by the constitution, any agreement that may be made would only affect direct taxes. With the federal government itself having access to this category of taxes, any settlement between the governments assumes there would be definition and acceptance of a rule of sharing which would suppress the ambiguities from which the constitutional practices of the past thirty years have resulted-
May I interpose here that of course the charge is that most of these ambiguities developed under the previous administration. I would imagine that the people who presented this report would see the Conservative government as a St. George killing these dragons of ambiguity. To continue:
We have already formulated this rule of sharing and it is deducible from the Constitution's general

The Budget-Mr. Fisher aims and purposes. Inasmuch as taxes have a qualitative relationship with the functions of collective life, (such relationship becoming more apparent as taxation becomes more onerous), they should be assigned, in a federative state, to the two orders of government according to the functions respectively vested in them. Thus, taxes on incomes affecting individuals and institutions should be reserved to the provinces, upon which devolves jurisdiction in cultural and social matters. On the other hand, since the federal government, for its part, is vested with the wider economic responsibilities, it should have sole access to taxes on goods and on the circulation of goods.
I want again to comment and say that if this is a good statement of the Quebec position or of the provincial position, and the minister spoke so strongly yesterday to stress the fact that his is not a centralizing government but that it is a government that has a respect for the provinces, I fail to see that within this present budget much consideration has been given to this matter and the stand of Quebec in relation to fiscal policies. I hope that in the future, as these two wings of Progressive Conservatives merge the Quebec viewpoint as expressed by the Tremblay report and the viewpoint of the people from what I might call outer Canada, the government will define more clearly just what it is going to do about the centralist position and whether it is going to be a centralist government or whether it is going to take the lead in financial matters to give the provinces back what the Quebec government in this report claimed was its right. In expressing my own opinion I might add that I hope the government does not make a retrograde step. I hope it leads these people from Quebec up to the view where they realize that the centralist position is the true position of this greater Canadianism that is now being broadcast and advanced so ably by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) of this country.
The minister made the point that no one had mentioned the magazine tax. I intended to mention the magazine tax. I felt all along that it was discriminatory; but I have never seen two better examples where I should like to see discrimination practised than in relation to Time magazine and Readers Digest. It has always seemed to me that Time magazine-and this applies in the United States as well as Canada-is a most retrograde form of journalism. You have opinionated conclusions presented in the form of what appears to be a news report. You have a continuous indoctrination. I wondered at the time when the tax was cancelled, at the fact that Time magazine in its indoctrination in its Canadian section has taken such a generally favourable view of the new government. But that probably is an unworthy suspicion.

With regard to gold, the minister felt that he had not received nearly enough recognition for the step he had taken there. I am pleased to recognize that step. What bothers me about this increase in the gold subsidy is this old question of private enterprise and free enterprise of which we are told consistently in this house. We just had it the other night, I believe, from the hon. member who defeated the former deputy leader of the C.C.F., stressing that his party is a party of free enterprise and private enterprise. It has always seemed to me to be most peculiar that this government would even consider extending this subsidy instead of wiping it out. Surely if you believe in free enterprise and private enterprise, and if this is the heart of your conviction, you do not want to subsidize and keep going something that cannot compete in the markets of the world.

I think they are admirable and I compliment the Minister of Finance on it. But I hope that some time, perhaps in the Conservative caucus, he might read a little lesson on the weakness of free enterprise and private enterprise in certain sectors of our economy and so explain to them that government action is not completely black and awful as many of the backbenchers especially seem to be putting forward here in this house.
I think one comment which the minister made is a very sound one. I think perhaps even members of my group and certain of

the Liberals have been unfair. He stressed that his government entered this house immediately following an election and that at that election they obtained a tremendous vote of confidence. I think that is a very sound argument. But I know the minister during his long stay in the opposition never allowed that matter to get in his way. I have checked the Hansard debates immediately after the 1949 election when the Liberal party was swept into power with such a great majority and I fail to find that he put halters on his tongue or took a very reticent part. He was extremely aggressive right after the election. I think that today we all acknowledge that certainly at this time his government has the confidence of the people.
I should also like to suggest to him-in contrast to what I have heard previous Conservative members say-that this budget has not gained a great deal of popularity in the country. It is not the most popular budget that has ever been brought down. There has been considerable criticism of it. Even such journals-righteous supporters of the government-as the Montreal Gazette have not been particularly kind to this budget or to the minister. I think that on this particular point he will have to recognize that we are just, in our poor and humble way, trying to carry out the duties of the opposition. If some of us are even taking his former actions in the opposition as a model, I hope that is not too hard on our dignity. I hope that he realizes that under it all we recognize that for a few moments and perhaps for another few months his party has the confidence of the country.
One of the points the minister stressed yesterday was that no one had come forward with any ideas to combat inflation; that here he had presented a budget, that inflation was one of the great problems of the country at the present time, and especially the Liberals had been retrograde in not coming forward with suggestions to stop this. There is a book that I have been reading-it was recently published-that has a number of suggestions on how to combat inflation. I should like to recommend it to the members of the house. It is a recent publication by a United States professor who had Canadian roots, namely J. Galbraith; it is called "The Affluent Society". There are a number of points from a commentary by another leading United States economist, Stuart Chase, on this book, that I think bear on this problem of inflation. This review from the Reporter magazine states:
Another important change has occurred in the conventional wisdom since Ricardo's time,-
For those who do not know who Ricardo was, may I say that he was an early 19th
The Budget-Mr. Fisher century economist who predicted the continuance of poverty and insecurity in the world.
-primarily as a consequence of the great depression. The goal of full employment and high wages is now supported by practically everybody in America.
And I would say in Canada.
How else indeed can the affluent society absorb its own production? This goal entails, however, a painful side effect in the wage-price spiral and more inflation. "Where inflation is concerned," Galbraith notes, "nearly everyone finds it convenient to confine himself to conversation."
It seems to me that the minister and the Prime Minister are wonderful at confining themselves to exhortative conversation, especially to labour groups with respect to combatting inflation. The article goes on:
"All branches of the conventional wisdom are equally agreed on the undesirability of any remedies that are effective." Effective means of combating inflation conflict with the ideal of production for the sake of full employment, and a bigger gross national product.
There is a theory that advancing the discount rate-
And this comes into the tight money policy idea as reflected in Canada-
-by the federal reserve will check inflation, but recent monetary history, alas, shows this to be an illusion. Such changes, furthermore, can be dangerous by checking business investment and encouraging unemployment, while administered prices soar majestically upward. The same attitudes that lead us to advocate full employment and the use of industrial plant at capacity "deny us the measures to prevent inflation." This is a shattering conclusion, but I am afraid it is true.
This is the comment of an economist upon one of the most important books on economics which has been published for some time. There is the question of inflation and the question of production, and the whole matter of how far we should push our gross national production. Should production, production, production be the only goal? One would almost gather that the minister thinks so, although I am sure that is not so. I know he is a man of religious conviction and I think he recognizes that there are many more important things in life than just pushing up our gross national product. I see, however, almost no recognition of this fact or of these other parts of life which are so important in this budget message which completely stresses the short range economic problems with which we find ourselves faced at the present time. Certainly in this budget there is no long range vision to pull us out of this inflationary spiral.
I think one of the brightest remarks made by Keynes, the economist, was that one of the difficulties in talking about short runs and long runs in economics is that in the long run we will all be dead. This is definitely

The Budget-Mr. Fisher a short run budget and there is no long range hope in this budget that we are going to snap out of this trend toward more and more inflation. The only solution the minister seems to have is the exhortatory one of admonition to the opposition.
Before leaving this subject I would like to refer to some recommendations made by Galbraith in order to get ourselves out of this particular rat trap into which our race to increase the gross national product has got us. I especially have in mind the first one, which I believe is well worth consideration by this government. I know it is an extraordinary measure, but I believe it is one which would do a great deal to snap us out of this condition and I suggest that the government particularly consider it if this winter turns out to be as bleak as some people predict.
Galbraith recommends firstly a flexible system of unemployment compensation, financed outside of actuarial standards by the federal government, on top of what provinces may do. As unemployment increases, scales of compensation go up until they are just under weekly earnings. As unemployment declines, scales go down. Thus, when jobs are plentiful the system will provide little incentive for malingering; when jobs are scarce no useful distinction can be made between those who are voluntarily idle and those unable to find work. A full head of consumer demand is meanwhile maintained and "the effect...is to make tolerable the unemployment which is associated with price stability." Galbraith says we cannot hope to check inflation without having some unemployment from time to time and that this is a fact which must be faced.
Galbraith goes on to make many other suggestions which I think would be equally applicable and one of them has always been a bane of the life of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming). This is that some form of limited price and wage controls should be instituted and a further step should be the automatic diversion of a share of the increasing income taxes to public authorities for public purposes.
I recommend that this analysis of what I would say is the North American economy and the difficulties in relation thereto should be considered together with some of the solutions suggested and that this will afford much assistance not only to members of parliament but to the Minister of Finance.
I would now like to refer to one point having to do with an omission in the budget, which I had hoped to see rectified. This matter has been taken up with the minister and I know he has his side of the story to tell. It has to do with an amendment which

was presented during the last parliament to the Income Tax Act providing as follows:
A person employed as a construction worker at a construction site from which he cannot reasonably be expected to return daily to his ordinary place of residence where he maintains a home in which he lives with his wife or other dependant shall not be required to include in income the value of free board and lodging furnished during the period of necessary absence or free transportation furnished to or from the construction site, or a reasonable allowance paid to him to cover expenses of such board and lodging or transportation.
During the last parliament the former member for Comox-Alberni and myself, together with the man who is now the leader of the Quebec Liberal party, pressed for this allowance to be extended to the loggers and bush workers in our country whose situation closely parallels that of the construction workers. A group of lumber workers in my area presented a brief to the Minister of Finance, and I must compliment the minister on the audience he gave us but the difficulty appears to hinge around this point: The construction workers who benefit from this particular amendment which was introduced comprise a very, very limited group. This legislation does absolutely nothing for the hourly wage earner; it applies only to people on salary and applies to the sort of executive or person on the managerial level. Very rarely does it help the bulk of the people working on a job. The fact remains that a bush worker or a logger in order to earn his income in most cases has to go away from his home and in effect maintain two domiciles or at least, if he is married, maintain a home in a town or village and also support himself on the job. He is unable to take advantage of this clause and even if the clause were to be extended to take care of loggers and bush workers it would not be of any assistance for the simple reason that under the contracts which apply in most cases in Canada between the unions and the employers in the woods industry there is no such thing as free board and lodging. The men pay for their board and lodging and the only way that any changes could be made which would prove effective for these men would be for the minister to bring in an amendment which would allow men living under these conditions, when they are maintaining a domicile in a city, to deduct what they pay for their board and lodging as an expense on their income tax returns.

How much of this charitable donation went to education we cannot be sure, but there are some figures which we can gather from previous years. The fact is that the corporations have not taken advantage even of the present tax situation. One wonders what they are going to do now that there is an additional 5 per cent. By law, corporations were permitted to deduct 5 per cent of their taxable income in respect of charitable donations. It dispelled an illusion to which they had clung obstinately. They had thought they could hold on in the province of Quebec, calling up, to gain confidence and save face after June 10, 1957, their triumphs of 1949 and of 1953. But they had forgotten that public opinion had changed since the days of 1948 when the population of Quebec was asked to forget the slaps in the face and the broken promises, as well as the war policy of the Mackenzie King government, and to support, in the name of race and religion, a fellow citizen of the same language and creed. Citizens of the province of Quebec and of Canada were right in then giving confidence to a man who proved himself a great Canadian. But it turned out that the Liberal government, even led by a great leader, abused its strength and lost touch with the people. That is why the people have withdrawn their confidence. It is then that the Quebec Liberals have believed, Mr. Speaker, that they could hold the province of Quebec by raising racial and religious prejudices.

Since his election at the head of the Conservative party, he has never ceased to advocate national unity. He has done so unremittingly by word and deed. For once, Canadians have the satisfaction of hearing the same

The Budget-Mr. Tremblay thing from one end of the country to the other. The province of Quebec, in particular, has not been favoured with a special and specious version of those words on unity. No one has tried to sell them a political idea through false pretenses. The same gospel of national unity, of harmony and co-operation "for a better Canada" has been preached. But they have been assured, this time with new emphasis, that the essential civic liberties would be respected and that the Canadian constitution would be, as it should, the guarantee of such liberties.
I recall that during the last electoral campaign, some newspapermen expressed their surprise that the Prime Minister was not making more promises to the province of Quebec. Liberal spokesmen instantly scented an easy and convenient trail. They started to blame the Conservatives for not making enough promises. But the electors were not fooled. They had too bitter memories of Liberal promises of a Canadian flag, of an ambassador to the Vatican and of bilingual cheques. Prime Minister as an enemy of the French Canadians in the province of Quebec. party against the person of the Prime Minister, and read abusive pamphlets against the religious and ethnical convictions of the hon. Prime Minister.

maintopic: CHRONOLOGICAL TABLE OF DUTIES AND TAXES ON AUTOMOBILES 1914 TO DATE
speechtext: Those are only quotations.

I have on file, Mr. Speaker, some of those publications. It is not for the purpose of reviving electoral quarrels that I report that attitude and that I speak as I do. It is for the purpose of inspiring our friends of the Liberal opposition with a certain form of caution in their criticism. Today they are playing the game of objectivity; they are criticizing the Conservative government. Yesterday, they were condemning the leader of the Conservative government. They tried to raise some doubts and some hard feelings towards the policy of the Conservative government. They carefully avoid mentioning that the electors refused to follow them in their attempts to discredit the hon. Prime Minister. It is to denounce such hypocrisy that I have spoken about those facts, as I do not want the public to be misled once more.
The electors of the province of Quebec voted for the Conservative party on the basis of its serious political program and its achievements. It would be an insult to their conscience to claim that they have yielded to all sorts of entreaties.
Instead, they ignored the calumnies which, -if not expressed openly at present by Liberal members from the province of Quebec, now in this house,-are not forgotten by those who heard them during the election campaign.

maintopic: CHRONOLOGICAL TABLE OF DUTIES AND TAXES ON AUTOMOBILES 1914 TO DATE
speechtext:
This is not the
provincial assembly.

speechtext:
Allow me to tell my hon. friends of the opposition who sent me this splendid red flower that I shall lay it on the grave of the Liberal party.
It is high time, Mr. Speaker, that some misconceptions which are fatal to good understanding between various racial groups of our country, be cleared. The sentence pronounced by the Canadian people, on March 31 last, shows eloquently that the electors of this country are enlightened judges of our political actions, and that we would be mistaken in trying to distract their attention from essential administrative problems. I am delighted because I see in this a sign of political maturity and the assurance that demagogues will no longer be listened to. At any rate, for the information of those who, a few years ago, denounced political immorality in our province and of those who make it

a point of discrediting our province, I might add that I do not understand why they are so slow in denouncing the campaign of racial and religious prejudice carried out by the Liberal party and of which the former member for Quebec-Montmorency has given now a too notorious example.
I know for sure that from now on Liberals will have to find other themes than those they have kept using in the province of Quebec to denounce the Conservative party and make it appear as a scarecrow synonymous with war, conscription, economic depression and racial and religious prejudice.

maintopic: CHRONOLOGICAL TABLE OF DUTIES AND TAXES ON AUTOMOBILES 1914 TO DATE
speechtext: And unemployment.

maintopic: CHRONOLOGICAL TABLE OF DUTIES AND TAXES ON AUTOMOBILES 1914 TO DATE
speechtext: On March 31 it was revealed how worn out were these old methods and how inefficient they had become. Liberals had to answer for their actions; the nation required of them an exact accounting of their stewardship. Such answer as they gave, no doubt, was far from being satisfactory to their accusers. To defame the Conservative party it was far too easy to talk of the 1917 conscription or of the depression of the thirties. The Liberals were far luckier than they deserved, in 1939, when the second world war brought an artificial prosperity to this country and seemed to demonstrate that they had been right in their statements against the Conservative party.

maintopic: CHRONOLOGICAL TABLE OF DUTIES AND TAXES ON AUTOMOBILES 1914 TO DATE
speechtext: Artificial for twenty years.

maintopic: CHRONOLOGICAL TABLE OF DUTIES AND TAXES ON AUTOMOBILES 1914 TO DATE
speechtext:
And it is largely because they failed to prepare Canada for normal conditions and for a peacetime economy, that this country now finds itself in a somewhat difficult position.
Whatever is done now in the way of rousing of anti-Tory feeling, whatever attempts are made to make a bogey out of the Conservative party, this will henceforth be no way to gain public support. Since the far-off days of 1917 and 1930, modern improvements have brought about a radical change in means of public information. No longer can anybody prevent people in British Columbia, for instance, from hearing, on the same day and at the same time, what is being said at the far end of Newfoundland. The provinces of this country are now in a position to speak to one another and it would be a very serious error to fail to take into account this factor of unity.
The Liberal party must therefore find something else to say. More particularly it must, as far as the province of Quebec is concerned, draw on resources other than those which it has exploited so far. No longer will it do to preach unilateral unity. Those tactics will have to be replaced by a truly national policy. I hope the Liberals in this
The Budget-Mr. Tremblay house realize that their present numbers, and the fact that they represent only a very few provinces, are the best possible demonstration of their party's failure in the national field. It should be sufficient to point out that close to one half of them represent the province of Quebec. Let them reflect on that fact, which confirms what I was saying about the events of 1949 and 1953, events which, while admirably serving their party, failed to assure its national survival. This might well be because the Liberal party has lost sight of its beginnings and did not remain faithful to its basic principles. It was to be the party of freedom and reform, as stated by Sir Wilfrid Laurier in a speech delivered on June 26, 1877. He said:
The policy of the Liberal party is to ensure the protection and defence of institutions, the spreading of influence, and-within the framework of these institutions-the development of our country's untapped resources. That is the Liberal party's policy; there is no other.
One can hardly deny that the Liberals of today have followed the downward trend. The twenty-two years of Liberal rule have belied the magnetism and the truth of Laurier's words. What it amounts to, Mr. Speaker, is that the Liberals of today are whittled-down Liberals, mere shadows of the Liberalism of former times-of that Liberalism which, judging by Sir Wilfrid Laurier's words, was indeed to bring about radical changes in Canadian institutions. But the Canadian Liberals were scared of the principles which they had borrowed from Europe; they wanted to water down, little by little, what was disquieting in their basic principles; they were afraid of going right through with it, of drawing the conclusions arising from their premises and of proving themselves to be true, strictly conforming Liberals. They did not have the courage of their political convictions. They ended up with that drab type of Liberalism, drained of its doctrinal content, with which we are familiar. And their principles are so inadequately given expression that it is difficult to associate Laurier with these politicians who have bartered their gospel of doctrinal Liberalism-which I do not approve of-for a vague creed of electoral opportunism.
Give me the Conservative tradition; it is based on the facts of history. The party of Macdonald and Cartier has never wished to break with tradition. It has not looked for a solution in historical continuity. It continued with its natural development within the constitutional framework of 1867. Never did it wish to blaze an unbroken trail, or advocate steps which were not in all respects in accord with the spirit and the letter of our constitutional instrument.

The Budget-Hon. P. Martin
I believe the strains we are feeling at the moment arise from the Liberal party having implemented an artificial constitutional evolution in Canada; and this political phenomenon finds its expression in the constitutional solutions of the Liberal party. That these solutions do not correspond wholly with the nature and the spirit of the British North America Act is the least that one must admit.
Thus it is, for instance, that the advocates of Canadian neo-Federalism try, by subtle means, to swing the pendulum of constitutional frictions. They would like to change an economic framework-in itself contingent upon, and subject to, the shifting conditions of our country's economy-for a constitutional formula-

In rising to take part in this very important budget debate I would like at the outset to say to my friend and classmate who has the great distinction of being the first Conservative in almost a quarter of a century to present a budget to this nation that, as one of his friends and contemporaries, I share his pride and his deep satisfaction in having that honour. I am sure that we in this house all recognize that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), a man of the greatest integrity and-as he once told us-a man of the greatest industry, would try to do all he could to present a budget which would satisfy a maximum number of citizens in this country.
However, while I congratulate my hon. friend on the great achievement that is his of being the first Tory in many years to present a budget in this house, I regret, also as a friend, that this particular budget should have so many shortcomings and that it will always be recognized as a budget presenting the greatest deficit in Canadian history.
My hon. friend yesterday did himself less than the justice one would have expected from the Minister of Finance under the circumstances. He admonished the opposition


because we had not indicated to him how savings might have been provided for and how the consequences of those savings might have been handed on to the Canadian people.
I would merely remind the minister as he himself reminded his predecessor, that no opposition is free from the obligation of making constructive suggestions from time to time.
But the primary obligation in the matter of the conduct of government in a country such as ours rests on the hon. gentlemen who sit on your right, Mr. Speaker.
Now the present Prime Minister (Mr. Die-fenbaker) said in this house in 1957 something which I think my distinguished friend the Minister of Finance might well wish to remember on this occasion. The present Prime Minister, who was then, of course, speaking on this side of the house, said:
I say to the government, if you would meet inflation, physician, heal yourself.

We have to cut down total spending where total spending exceeds our productive capacity. Cuts are imperative.
I would remind the Minister of Finance of these words. The leader of the opposition concluded, in 1957, by saying:

The Budget-Hon. P. Martin

maintopic: CHRONOLOGICAL TABLE OF DUTIES AND TAXES ON AUTOMOBILES 1914 TO DATE
speechtext:
The main criticism I have to make is that in the face of current economic conditions, in the face of the present abnormal level of unemployment in this country and in terms of what I contend to be a developing trend in unemployment which may be more serious than what we have experienced up to now, this government, through its Minister of Finance and through this budget, has not appreciated the seriousness of the economic situation which now confronts this country and which, I am going to argue, will face us with increasing severity in the months ahead.
The other day we asked, through a motion put forward by the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), for the economic survey for 1958, and the Prime Minister, resisting that motion, said it was a secret document. He did not use the phrase that it was a hidden document, but he said it was a document confidential in character which, because of the public interest, could not be given to the Canadian parliament or to the Canadian people at this time.
Mr. Speaker, we have the right to ask of this government whether these budgetary policies as presented by the Minister of Finance represent the advice given to the government by its financial officers, by its trade officials, by officials in the Bank of Canada and others in the public service competent to advise the ministry in matters of this sort. We have the right to suspect in the face of many indications that this budget does not represent all of that opinion and all of that advice. We have grounds for suspecting greatly that this government in its budget ignores the financial situation which now confronts the nation and which is likely to confront it in the months ahead. Hon. members will not forget how on January 20 last, the present Prime Minister, speaking in this house said, as recorded on page 3522 of Hansard:
My hon. friend said there are problems today that were not even contemplated last June. I intend to establish as clearly as the printed word will make possible that during the months of March, April, May until June 10, my hon. friends concealed from the Canadian people the facts.
Then at page 3526, the same right hon. gentleman, speaking of this confidential document, this secret document, this hidden report which continues to be produced by the Department of Trade and Commerce and which has been denied to us by the right hon. gentleman in 1958, said;
They went ahead with the policy which could not but accelerate the forces that were bringing about a deflationary condition in Canada. I am going to now read from this document in order to answer my hon. friend who the other night said, "In

The Budget-Hon. P. Martin June there was no problem of unemployment; our trade was at the highest level; we had an expanding economy."
Today one looks back and realizes that these men who were in power did not do that of which my hon. friend spoke in such colourful terms the other night. He said we must not conceal facts, but I put it to the hon. members opposite- every one of them in the official opposition-that they hid the facts; they concealed the record; they did not let the Canadian people know what was taking place.

maintopic: CHRONOLOGICAL TABLE OF DUTIES AND TAXES ON AUTOMOBILES 1914 TO DATE
speechtext: A good speech.

maintopic: CHRONOLOGICAL TABLE OF DUTIES AND TAXES ON AUTOMOBILES 1914 TO DATE

Someone says, "A good speech". Yes, it was a good speech and because it was a good speech I am now using it as a basis for the action I am going to ask the Minister of Finance to take. If it was right for the Prime Minister in January of 1958 to embark on the unprecedented step of divulging to this house a document marked confidential and secret that had been prepared by one department of government dealing with the economic situation of the country, does any hon. member deny that it is right that this house should now ask the present Prime Minister to now reveal to this parliament and to this nation the economic survey presented by the Department of Trade and Commerce to this government in 1958?
The former minister of finance, Mr. Harris, in his budget speech in 1957 did not dodge the implications of this so-called secret, hidden report which the previous government, in the language of the present Prime Minister, "refused to give parliament" and the current counterpart of which that same right hon. gentleman now refuses in 1958 to disclose to each and every one of us so that we can ascertain the extent to which the Minister of Finance properly carries out the recommendations and the policies of Her Majesty's advisors in Canada. What was right in 1957 regarding the document known as the economic survey by the same logic must continue to be valid in 1958.
In 1957 Mr. Harris, the then minister of finance, did not overlook the danger signs outlined in the so-called secret, hidden document which the present Prime Minister placed on the table of this house at our insistence once he had made reference to it. The minister of finance in 1957 clearly took cognizance of that report. In fact he used practically some of the very words contained in it indicating the seriousness of the situation as the authors of this report saw developing.
