As I have said, this publication was issued months ago by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. It forecast a decline of 3 per cent in capital expenditures, a point which my hon. friend the Minister of Finance did not underline at all.
I have spent some time on the economic survey of 1958 and on the right of parliament, in light of last year's precedent, to know what that document contains. Does it reflect the judgment of those impartial bodies such as the Canadian Tax Foundation, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and the very excellent study on unemployment made by the Canadian Labour Congress? Does it reflect the attitude of the Department of Labour? I suggest to the Minister of Finance that the reason the Prime Minister refused to give the house the 1958 economic survey is because that survey does not support the main lines taken by the Minister of Finance

in his budget, a budget that denies the critical seriousness of present and future unemployment levels.
The Minister of Finance was the last minister in the government to acknowledge last fall and last January that there was a serious problem of unemployment. The Minister of Finance by this budget completely ignores the recession which Canadians are experiencing. The minister seemingly is gambling on the possibility of a sudden upturn which we all trust will eventuate. I am going to suggest, in anticipating the kind of argument that will be made by those who do not like a realistic appraisal of the economic situation as one sees it in the country, that I sincerely hope the upturn in our country will be such as to warrant the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) being able to refer to low unemployment rolls and to show a minimum number of unplaced applicants under the national employment service. I earnestly trust that the export position of this country will improve. I hope that no hon. member will say that because the facts do not seem to support this kind of assessment we are not doing our duty to the nation when we, as well as impartial observers, indicate how completely out of step this budget is with realities in our country at the present time.
The acting minister of labour tabled the other day some figures showing 366,000 persons unemployed and 607,000 unplaced applicants in the last reported month. I suggest that the gap between these two figures, the number of unplaced applicants and the actual jobless, is so great as to warrant the dominion bureau of statistics taking a second look at them and seeing whether or not the gap which is unusually large does not represent a much greater margin of error than can reasonably be expected through the sampling process. I realize that the estimate of the dominion bureau of statistics is based on a small sample survey taken each month and it is possible that a greater than average margin of error was experienced in May which could possibly account for the disparity. In any event, 366,000 persons out of work in the month of May represents a serious economic situation in a country like Canada particularly at that period of the year.
When one adds to this figure the numbers of others who are unemployed but who are not reported in the dominion bureau of statistics standards as being unemployed one realizes that my statement is by no means an exaggeration. The dominion bureau of statistics does not include as unemployed a man who works only half an hour a week; it does not include people who are engaged for less
The Budget-Hon. P. Martin than 30 hours a week; it does not include those who will be called back to work within a limited time. Therefore, applying the lowest estimate to the month of May, the Minister of Finance I am sure will not deny that that represents a serious unemployment situation. It represents a figure more than double what it was in the preceding year and in the corresponding period.
I said earlier that I did not believe the Minister of Finance has taken into account in his calculations the advice given to him by his own officials. I do not say positively that that is the case but from everything that one can see, from pronouncements made by independent bodies, whose job and whose interest it is to make compilations of future trends, one comes to the conclusion that either the Minister of Finance has completely shut himself off from those who advise him or he is taking the great gamble of being overly optimistic in the hope that his gamble might work. That is a dangerous course for any minister of finance to take.

speechtext: The house resumed consideration of the motion of Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means.

speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of National Revenue):
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker this afternoon, just before the dinner recess, we were treated to a flow of eloquence forcefully delivered in the best traditions of a histrionic display: the dark clothes, the flashing eyes, the sombre voice. All that was needed was the black cap and we would have had the judge pronouncing sentence of death on the Canadian economy. It was a type of delivery which was somewhat wasted in the House of Commons and which might better have been employed in the theatre at Stratford where I am sure the hon. gentleman could obtain employment to a very high degree. I am not sure just what histrionic display is going to follow it but I know that it will not be given in any such funereal language. However, I am sure that another will paint as sombre
The Budget-Mr. Nowlan and lugubrious a scene. Perhaps for a few moments, Mr. Speaker, moving between these pictures of gloom and doom, we may come back to the facts of the budget and deal with these for a short time.
Much has been said in this debate of a critical nature. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) has been criticized. We have sat here for eight days listening to the debate, the contents of which the house well knows. This is not one of those sensational earthshaking budgets, that provokes great headlines in the press but it is a budget, as the Minister of Finance said at the outset when he delivered his speech, that has produced many matters of benefit to many Canadians. I am not dealing now with the general economic policy but with the specific matters in the budget to which I think attention should be called for a moment in passing.
One of these comes under the department which I happen to administer, namely that of national revenue and has an impact with respect to income tax. From the time I came into the office which I now hold I was impressed by the number of letters-not running into the thousands, but perhaps 500 or 1,000; something of that nature-which were sent to the minister complaining of the application of the act in so far as income tax reductions were concerned in connection with drugs. You all know the situation there. There is in the Income Tax Act a provision that when medical expenses exceed 3 per cent of the income, these deductions can be made for income tax purposes. Under the preceding administration, as the act was administered heretofore, those drugs had to be enumerated and specified by the Department of National Health and Welfare. Then when that was done a deduction could be made for those purchases. As I said, many of the letters received from the ordinary citizens of this country, from parents with children who were desperately ill; from people who had relatives who needed the most expensive drugs in order to recover, and where recovery was perhaps not always certain, they were pathetic letters-I think that is the only word that can be used to describe them-in which they suggested that some change should be made whereby they could obtain deductions for these drugs which are prescribed today by doctors and which were outside the very limited number which had been prescribed by the Department of National Health and Welfare. Even under the more efficient administration of my colleague, the present Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Monteith), we did not find that we could give the deductions that I felt were necessary.
In consultation with the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Health and

The Budget-Mr. Nowlan Welfare it was decided, as you know, to include in the budget a provision whereby drugs bought on doctor's prescription could hereafter qualify for a deduction in this regard. We trust the medical profession. We know that provision will not be abused. This, Mr. Speaker, is a simple illustration of what has been done in this budget. Simple, common sense, matter of fact changes are made here and there which affect the lives of thousands of Canadians across this country and which reflect tremendous credit on the Minister of Finance who prepared that budget and who brought it into the House of Commons.
I can think of another provision under the Income Tax Act which does not affect thousands, but does probably affect tens of thousands of Canadians. The one I have in mind I have myself encountered many times. I am sure all lawyers who have had the good fortune to practise in rural communities will also have faced it. I have in mind the family where the parents are getting old and they want to have their son remain on the farm and they convey the farm over to him as an inducement to him to remain there, not thinking of the application of the Income Tax Act and not thinking of the provisions with respect to the gift tax. Having done so, they then find one, two, three or sometimes even five years later, after the father has died and it has become impossible to change the situation, that a gift tax has been imposed sometimes running into thousands of dollars.
Then there is the case of the husband and wife who are perhaps retiring, perhaps establishing a home somewhere else and knowing that there will sooner or later be a death but who want to maintain a home so as to avoid the payment of gift tax, succession duty and so on and so forth. The husband has earned the money and has paid for the house but, if it were under a joint ownership arrangement, all sorts of problems arise with respect to taxes.
Under the budget which has been brought down we have a provision whereby the farmer or the father-not necessarily a farmer, of course-can convey property to his son or to his daughter and avoid payment of the gift tax. Similarly, a husband can convey his property to be held under a joint ownership by himself and his wife and can also avoid the tax and all the incidental obligations which arise upon the death of one or other of the parties. Here, again, is a very simple illustration of what I mean when I say that this budget, although it has not made the headlines with respect to these matters I have mentioned, has

affected the lives of many thousands of people in this country and has very favourably affected those lives.
Take next the matter of the sales tax. We have been asked what we have done for the municipalities-have we forgotten the municipalities, and someone over on the other side of the house will say, "Hear, hear". When we were on the other side of the house we urged the government for years and years to do something about the relaxation of sales taxes on purchases made by municipalities and when we made such suggestions we were treated with scornful contempt. It was impossible to consider such a thing. This budget has made provision in this respect. There is wide provision for sales tax exemption on purchases made by municipalities, particularly in those fields which are important to municipalities in these times; for instance, with respect to the problems of pollution, sewage disposal and all those matters which are today bearing so heavily upon the municipalities. There is a provision in this budget whereby they will save millions of dollars, even on the present scale of purchases, and as the years go by there will be more and more savings.
With respect to institutions, whereas formerly there was a narrow list certified by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, the provisions for institutions are now immeasurably widened so far as sales tax exemptions are concerned.
There is a simple little problem which has created so much hardship and difficulty which has also been provided for, and that is with respect to school authorities across this country, from Vancouver to Halifax. Protests have rolled in-I have seen scores of them in the short time during which I have been in office-complaining of the effect of taxes on school purchases for furniture and the fact that exemptions apply only to that furniture specifically designed for schools. Scores of school boards have had to pay sales tax on items which they very properly thought would have been free of such tax. This condition has now been rectified and I know the provisions of this budget will mean tremendous savings to school boards throughout the country.
I could go on and on to list examples of measures which will ensure tremendous savings to the people concerned and which are of great importance to them, but there is one, perhaps very minor item, which I would like to mention which has certainly been a source of great irritation to the public in the past. There was an imposition of a fee of $2 imposed upon businessmen for a licence to collect the sales tax from themselves for the government. While this $2

fee was not a very important factor, perhaps, I do not know of anything which has created more irritation among businessmen. A simple little change has been made and this fee has been done away with.
I have not exhausted the list of benefits under this budget by a long shot but I would now like to turn to some of the many criticisms we have heard. Firstly, we have heard that this is a high tariff budget; we have had a somber picture painted for us of high tariff walls being erected, shades of Bennett being invoked and references to Tory policies in the past. We are told that this country is now facing high tariffs as a result of the budget which has been brought down.
One such reference will be found at page 1538 of Hansard for June 23, 1958, where the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate spoke of the tariff provisions as follows:
-I do not know that I should call it a Bennett provision because Mr. Meighen tried it before him and it was repealed once before by the Liberals before Bennett-is, of course, of all the protective devices the most insidious and the most dangerous.
We are all of course familiar with the imagination of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate in portraying the pictures in his mind. Sometimes when I hear him speaking I am reminded of that house that Jack built, the house which had a little malt in it, a little rye in it, a little straw in it and all the rest of it, and finally it fell down. That was the house that Jack built, and that is the way it is with the house of high tariffs, which this Jack has built, because there is absolutely nothing in the budget which in any way reflects high tariffs.
There are five classes of changes in the budget, five minor classes, with respect to tariff changes and four of these were recommended by the tariff board. The minister is accused of being a high tariff Tory; this government is being accused of raising the tariffs as high as Hamono's gallows.
What would have been the accusation, what would have been the criticism if we had failed to accept the recommendations of the tariff board. We would have been criticized and attacked for not recognizing the impartial judgment of that great tribunal. The minister has now done this and we are criticized for these so-called high tariffs. I do not think anyone seriously objects to the revision with respect to steel products. The iron and steel amendments are long overdue as the last revision was issued 28 years ago, while today there has been a tremendous expansion in the development of all primary and secondary steel industries in Canada.
The Budget-Mr. Nowlan The great majority of the amendments, however, are merely for purposes of simplification; some are for reduction and there are very, very few limited increases.
It is the same situation with respect to the pipe and tube schedule; it is almost entirely a matter of adjustment and simplification. It is also the same with respect to woollens. We have heard a great deal about the increase in the tariff on woollens; this increase was also recommended by the tariff board and we were confronted with that recommendation.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You asked for it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We asked for it. The matter had been referred to the tariff board. Sure, we got their recommendation but what is the tariff board for? Did the hon. gentleman opposite raise tariffs without the recommendation of the tariff board? Did they ignore such recommendations? Of course they did not.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We reduced them.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, and we have reduced them too. We have reduced far more in this budget than we have increased, make no mistake about that. The increase on woollens, on a yardage basis, means only a few cents on the amount of cloth going into a suit of clothes.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Why do it at all, then?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Because we had a recommendation from the tariff board and we followed that recommendation. That is why we did it. There is certainly ample justification for the increase, as the tariff board has established, and I wonder if hon. members on the other side of the house are questioning that. If they are I would like to hear about it. So much for tariff increases, the ones specifically named in the budget.
There has also been much talk about the practice of the department with respect to evaluation. It is true that we have increased the evaluation staff of the department. Prior to the war the previous government had 45 or 50 evaluators, highly trained appraisers in most of the ports of the world, making examination of goods coming into Canada. The war came and most of these men, practically all of them, were brought back to Ottawa. Because of their skill and experience they were given senior jobs here, and the net result was that after the war there was practically no one left at all who had had any training in the appraisals branch except the senior executive officials in headquarters in Ottawa. In those days the market was such that everybody was buying, regardless, and it was not necessary to fill up these staffs.

The Budget-Mr. Nowlan Today the situation is different and we have got 45 or 50 appraisers, university men, largely, who are being trained so that they may strengthen the staff and carry out the appraisals which are necessary if Canadian industry is going to be protected from superficially low values.
An ad valorem tariff can be easily nullified if the values are reduced to such an extent that they have no basis in actuality. After all, the term "fair market value" must surely have some meaning, and it must be remembered that it has been determined time and time again that the market value has really had no reference whatsoever to fair market value and that anyone by making a few sales in the country of origin could then send the goods here, avoiding dumping duty. And when such goods are sold superficially below cost they threaten not only Canadian industry but, what is more important, the employees of Canadian industry.
We heard a prophecy this afternoon of dire doom with respect to unempolyment and the great extent to which it was going to increase in this country. I sat the other morning in the railway committee room and listened to Mr. Burt and the other spokesmen from the delegation that came from Windsor and Hamilton representing the unemployed and demanding government action. What was the principal thing which they demanded? They demanded that we take tariff action to keep out importations from, in particular, the United States. They said, and I am not passing judgment on the correctness of their statement, that the importation of automobiles, the importation of automobile parts, the importation of machinery, all these things had increased substantially, and contributed to unemployment in Canada. They urged us to take action so that these goods could be manufactured in Canada and provide employment for Canadian workmen rather than that they be made in some other country.
I wonder whether the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) who was so eloquent this afternoon on the subject of unemployment will give the government his support when the motion comes before the House of Commons to provide for a different basis of fixing valuations. I presume we can count on his full support and on the support, also, of the party to your left, Mr. Speaker, whose spokesmen were so eloquent on this subject in the House of Commons the other day.
And now, with regard to this so-called high tariff policy. There is no high tariff policy in so far as actual tariff changes are concerned. None whatever. And the change as far as increasing the staff is concerned is something going back to the practice which was carried on by hon. members opposite prior

to the war, and they profess to be a low tariff party, not a high tariff party. And the changes in valuation which were suggested by the Minister of Finance, and which I hope to have the honour to introduce in this house before very long, is one change and one change only; not an invidious change or something which would alter the whole economic structure of this country, but one which will help to deal with the unemployment situation, because goods are being brought into this country at fictitious values, often below the cost of production. We intend to do something about this and ensure that we at least give some protection to Canadians in this country.
What else do the critics say about this budget? They say it is a deficit budget. Sure it is a deficit budget. We have a deficit. The hon. member for Essex East this afternoon took off the judge's robes for a moment and assumed the mantle of a prophet and predicted that the budget deficit this year would be way over what the Minister of Finance had suggested, and called in aid several organizations to support his contention.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

As for Mr. Mackenzie King, your revered leader, listen to what he said: "The Liberal party has to go through the valley of humiliation." As long as members of that party keep talking about two faces and blaming the people of Canada for being fooled, the people of Canada will continue to be fed up with them and they will sit there until your great grandchildren have grown beards.

Mr. Speaker, I know that my time is running out much more rapidly than I realized, and I have to pass on to other matters. There are many other things which have been said about this budget, and again I refer to our friend with the Puckish sense of humour, and the house that Jack built. I believe that all parties In this parliament and most Canadians share the view that the national budget is no longer merely a matter of the government accounts that should be balanced every 12 months on some financial rule of the thumb. We view the national budget now as an integral part of the nation's business, influenced by and having an influence upon the state of employment, income and prices.

You may think so, my friend. We also know, and every hon. member will admit it I am sure, that the economy of this country is difficult to administer. Canada is a vast country covering an enormous area stretching from the Atlantic to the Pacific and embracing areas stretching from the temperate zone to the Arctic zone. It is not as easy a country to administer as is that to the south which is, as it were, a self-contained empire embracing a tropical and temperate climate. One would assume that the situation in the United States would be much better than the situation that obtains here particularly in view of all the mismanagement in Canada about which we have heard and also because of the fact that hon. gentlemen opposite tie our economy to the coat tails of the United States economy so it is hard to divorce ourselves from it even if we wanted to. We know what the facts have been down through the years. When the United States economy went up, the Canadian economy also went up, but not quite so high because we ride on its coat tails and when the United States economy went down our economy went down further and faster. That has been our history and I do not think any one can question it.
It would be interesting at this point to glance briefly at a comparison of indices between the two countries. I hasten to admit at the outset, as was pointed out this afternoon by the hon. member for Essex East, that motor vehicle production in Canada has fallen considerably below that in the United States as is also the case with regard to pulp production which is a large industry in this country. In that case, too, we have fallen below the United States. But let us examine some of the other indices that are available. Are we really sustaining hard times, a depression? What about business failures? Surely there must be a vast number in Canada as compared with the United States. The index reveals that in

based on dominion bureau of statistics figures so hon. gentlemen opposite will not quarrel with their authenticity.

Those, Mr. Speaker, are some of the factors with respect to economic conditions in this country at the moment. I could go on at length but I do not want to take more time in dealing with this matter. It is quite true, Mr. Speaker, the house would not wish him to repeat what he said on that occasion because repetition of nothing by nothing does not add very much to our knowledge. We had hoped that perhaps the Minister of Finance on this occasion, the budget occasion, would have said something about this problem. We must not speak or criticize because of the last election; we must not fight the last election over again in

Anyway, the last thing in the world that the Minister of Finance should reproach us for is discussing the last election. Nor has he any right to draw from that the conclusion that we have no right to criticize the government.
Indeed the Minister of Finance last night began to fight the next election, in that connection he made one statement which on reflection I hope he will withdraw. He said there was no member-and he mentioned especially on this side, the member for Villeneuve (Mr. Dumas)-who had not the decency-that was not the word he used- who had shown any appreciation of what the government had done in this budget through the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act, and he mentioned the hon. member for Villeneuve. Perhaps he thought in doing that he would help his party in the next election. If he had looked at Hansard- he should have looked at it before he made this reference-he would have found the hon. member for Villeneuve spoke in the budget debate at page 1617 of Hansard, where he had this to say:

Well, Mr. Speaker, we will let that pass. This budget speech of the minister is a fascinating thing to study in the light of perhaps what I may be permitted to call certain Fleming fixations in the years before 1958. The first and most important fixation in those years-I wish the minister would read some of his old speeches-was that the budget must be balanced. There must be neither deficits in difficult times through tax cuts to stimulate the economy nor must there be surpluses in boom times as a hedge against inflation and for debt reduction. Down, he so often said-and his words at that time were often very vigorous

-with cyclical budgeting as an instrument of the devil and Douglas Abbott, the Douglas Abbott who was quoted with so much approval by the Minister of National Revenue a few moments ago. Budgets must be balanced.
Well, Mr. Speaker, what have we now? The old Conservative orthodoxy has been thrown to the winds and the minister is now in direct and startling contradition with his former statements. He is forced and is trying to defend now what he used to condemn as heresy, the Liberal theory of budgetary policy which was stated a few moments ago by the Minister of National Revenue. In other words, he is favouring now deficit financing and we are glad indeed to welcome him into that fold. But to be logical and responsible the minister must also admit now that surpluses, debt reduction and credit restrictions may also be desirable in circumstances when expansion seems to be leading to inflation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

How? It could be done easily-Mr. Drew used to wax eloquent on this-by eliminating waste and extravagance. They said that $500 mil- ' lion in tax reductions should come out of such savings and reduced expenditure. Why, the hon. member for Greenwood, Minister without Portfolio, had this to say in the house on April 5, 1955, as found at page 2765 of Hansard:
-tax reductions . . . should not come out of deficits; they should not have to be borrowed . . . We should get tax reductions from savings of expenditures-
Two years later, on March 19, 1957, he had this to say as found at page 2464 of Hansard: Everyone who is not a moron knows that it- Government spending.
-could be cut down.
Well, Mr. Speaker, what has happened to that doctrine? Look at the estimates. They are the highest in our history. What about waste and extravagance? It was said that savings could be made to bring these figures 57071-3-120
The Budget-Mr. Pearson down even in a time of emergency and recession and how is this unprecedented increase in our estimates regarded? As something to be deplored? Not at all. Here are the minister's own words in his speech a couple of weeks ago. As found on page 1232 of Hansard he had this to say:
Government expenditures contributed to the maintenance of economic activity. At all three levels of government they rose by almost seven per cent despite some decline in defence expenditures.
Again, on page 1235 he said that now that business is slowing down "we shall be able to devote more of our energies to filling some of the gaps which have developed... in housing, in municipal services and in other requirements for social capital in Canada, and in laying the basic foundations for the new period of business expansion which will not be long delayed." speechtext:
The minister has also boasted of the superb timing in the government's threefold approach to the twin problems of recession and inflation. He said the other night that this policy had just the right balance, and I think I am quoting him accurately when I say that he said "it is the

The Budget-Mr. Pearson best mix of the various means" applied in a timely fashion. Well, Mr. Speaker, it is a mix all right. It is a mix concocted in the last 12 months of a variety of political ingredients applied as and when political considerations seemed to dictate, applied bit by bit, dissipating and minimizing the effect on employment which a budget with a planned, co-ordinated, comprehensive system of tax reduction brought in last autumn would have had. Only now, in June and July of this year, does the government, rationalizing after the event, discover an economic purpose for steps which it took for political reasons. Only now is it trying to make an economic virtue out of political necessity.
If we look at the true size of the deficit we will all agree that the minister is certainly practising his new cyclical religion with the zeal of a convert, if not with the wisdom of the experienced worshipper. But surely he must know, if he is a student of these matters at all, and I assume he gets good advice on them, that during periods of declining economic activity in the private sector of the economy, maintaining the stability of employment and income requires more than a huge budgetary deficit. Anti-cyclical policy would be too easy to apply if it could be reduced to that simple formula. The timing of the deficit, the method by which it is brought about and its size in relation to the national product are of very great importance indeed if a reasonable degree of economic stability is to be achieved or is to be maintained.
Above all, government fiscal policy must be based on a realistic assessment of economic conditions themselves. Now, Mr. Speaker, I am sure that even the minister will readily admit that his deficit was not planned and timed on any such rational assessment of current economic conditions. It is not leading to any new policy designed and adequate to cope with the present situation. It is merely, as I have said, as a result of the implementation of some electoral promises made when economic conditions were much different from what they are today.
Indeed, as we have said on this side time and time again, this huge deficit was implicitly contained in the Conservative program presented during the election of a year ago in June. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, while this 1957 Conservative program was being implemented in part during the last session,-and I emphasize the words "in part"-no indication of any planned or comprehensive action to deal with the recession was given by the government at this time. Indeed, the measures then introduced could not have been initiated by the government to deal with increasing unemployment, because almost until the very
[Mr. Pearson. 1
end of the last session the ministers denied- and they denied it repeatedly in this house- that a serious economic situation was developing. As a result we now have a built-in deficit created on the spur of the political moment. The attempt made by the minister to give us a post mortem rationalization of the sporadic action taken by the government will not change the facts.
Therefore it is not the deficit as such that we are criticizing, because deficits are required in the kind of situation we have in this country at the present time. Even though this deficit represents a complete reversal of financial and economic policy on the part of those who are bringing it in, it is not that which we are criticizing so much as the method or rather the lack of method used by the government in bringing it about. Furthermore, most of the additional items responsible for this deficit-except, of course, the drop in tax yields-constitute long term commitments which the government will find almost impossible to reduce if the economic climate were to change in the next few years, as we all hope it will not change. I recognize of course, as my party did at the time, that most of these items-tax cuts, increased social security benefits and the others-might well have been desirable in themselves for social or humanitarian reasons. But there was no possibility whatever at that time of considering them also in the framework of the economic outlook and of their long term inflationary implications.
The government systematically refused last autumn to present to the house a realistic assessment of the economic position or to give us a proper national accounting. Surely all must now realize that as a result of the unrelated actions, or perhaps I had better say as a result of the action related only to the political situation taken at that time by the government, new and important financial rigidities have been introduced into our economic structure which, in the minister's own words, have planted an inflationary time bomb which might later go off with a dangerously explosive effect. That is a very graphic way of putting it.
Believe me, Mr. Speaker, all this is very different indeed from the planned and coordinated tax cuts applied in a manner and in a place where they could give the maximum impetus to the economy and to employment. That is what we proposed in the last election campaign as something which should have been done by this government last autumn. We stand by those proposals today. We certainly do not apologize for them in any way, shape or form. They were proposals which

at that time were considered to be economically sound by some of the best economic thinkers in this country.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not by the people.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They were proposals put forward in the midst of a grave unemployment situation and, as I have just said, without any benefit of a national accounting by the government or without complete and full information either of the economic situation or of the government's policy with regard to it which we should have had in the House of Commons last autumn. As a comprehensive and co-ordinated emergency unemployment program they made sense. In the eyes of the economic and financial experts in this country they made far more sense than did the sporadic and unrelated approach made by the government to this problem at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
But not to the
people.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It was certainly not our fault that they could not put them forward last autumn or early this spring within the framework of a budget and a national accounting. That national accounting should have been given in view of the promises made during the election campaign a year ago and in view of the attacks made on the monetary and fiscal policies of the previous government. It had been definitely promised by the minister himself. If that had been done, and it was not done-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It was not
promised.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The promise has been put on the record in this house at least half a dozen times. If words mean anything at all-and perhaps they do not mean very much to my hon. friend-those words mean that he did promise to introduce a budget into the house at the last session.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I deny that.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The record will have to speak for itself, Mr. Speaker. If that had been done Canadians at that time would have been able to form an idea of the course to be followed by the government and the proposals from other parties could have been made and considered in the light of a full knowledge of the situation. But no such action was taken.
What did we learn from the minister last December about the situation in this country? The estimate of his predecessor, Mr. Harris, of revenue was $5,170 million, made in March, 57071-3-120i
The Budget-Mr. Pearson 1957, and he accepted that estimate of revenue. Last December it was accepted. That will be found at page 2002 of Hansard. The other day in the house he told us that no substantial reduction in revenue was likely except from the 1957 tax reduction. We were told that. This is the kind of information on which we had to make up our minds and base our policies. What were the facts? Revenue dropped $510 million to $4,660 million and much of that drop-more than half of it- had nothing to do with tax reductions. As for expenditures, these were $534 million higher in spite of all the Tory talk about reducing expenditures, which talk was repeated by the minister himself on December 6 and, if he likes, he can read it at page 2003 of Hansard in order to refresh his memory of what he said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am sure the hon. gentleman does not wish to be unfair but he purports now to be quoting figures given by me last December which were with reference to the fiscal year 1957-58. But by a peculiar form of elision he slipped on to say that the revenue receipts were $4,660 million. Those are for the fiscal year 1958-59 and are an estimate.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am not misquoting, Mr. Speaker, and I am not misunderstanding the minister. Surely he does not deny that revenue dropped last year from the figure which Mr. Harris gave us in the spring and which he accepted as the estimate of revenue last December.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It did not drop to $4,660 million.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It was on the basis of his acceptance of those figures that we have to operate at this stage and in spite of that information which we got and which did not turn out to be accurate information. Of course, I do not expect the minister to be infallible and omniscent in these matters.
he expenditures now proposed, however, are far from anything that any one on this side could possibly have anticipated in the previous session of parliament, provided we believed in any way, shape or form the figure which they gave us and their protestations of cuts in expenditure. The result of all this was that Mr. Harris estimated for last year a surplus of $151 million, leaving out the $100 million which my hon. friend always added to that surplus. Even at the end of January of this year, the Minister of Finance insisted that this surplus, which he called a respectable surplus, would be achieved by what he called prudent management. That will be found at page 4019 of Hansard. We learned in June of this year that the position was

The Budget-Mr. Pearson very different indeed and that instead of this respectable surplus which was to be achieved by prudent management, we got a deficit of $39 million. This was the kind of information, or these were the facts on which we on this side had to operate in working on our financial and tax policies for a recession.
Now let me come to a third and very fierce fixation held by the minister and which I think has now been liquidated by the responsibility of office. It often has a salutary and liquidating effect. This fixation is the vicious effect of so-called tight money on the business and economic situation last spring.
Tight money, that was the culprit! The Liberal culprit responsible for the pause, the slowdown, unemployment and everything else that was bad. The Liberals did it all.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As a result of their tight money policy they were responsible for everything.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is just what I had hoped to hear; that is the way the fable goes. It continues that the tight money policy was the culmination of those years of misrule.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Those years of misrule under which Canada became the most envied country in the world, achieving a position of wealth, power and high respect unparalleled in its history, which the minister well knows, because outside this country he acknowledges it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: In his speeches he acknowledges it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister should read his own speeches, particularly the one made in Florida last year.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He acknowledges the fact that our country is envied and has been for years the envy of all other countries in the world.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It has been envied a great deal more since June 10, 1957.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We have now come to the end of this ten year period-and what a period of time it was. It was a period, to use the words of an hon. member-I believe from Nova Scotia-when he was speaking the other night, of wounds and scars. Wounds and scars on a national economic body which during those years was perhaps the healthiest national economy in the world.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nonsense.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Don't take my word for it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Don't worry, we won't.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will quote an authority far more impressive to hon. members opposite than myself, namely, the Minister of Finance himself. In his budget speech reported in Hansard at page 1237 for June 17, 1958 he talks about the rapid development which has been taking place in the Canadian economy in recent years. He also refers to Canada's rapid economic growth of recent years. How did we manage to accomplish this rapid economic development in Canada at a time of such terrible misrule? Does this sound as if the Tory government inherited a decaying country, weakened and destroyed by Liberal misrule. The minister is right when he speaks like this, and he is wrong when he talks the other way on the hustings, and he knows it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I talk the same way everywhere, and you know it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What, then, caused the
recession?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You caused it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is the trouble with some hon. members, that they can think in no other terms than party politics, but times are a little too serious for that kind of political party	approach.	At the	beginning	of the
election campaign on February 14-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We are not supposed to be talking about the election campaign.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-I said	the	cause	of the
economic recession-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Perhaps	my	hon.	friendswho have not spoken in	the	debate would
kindly wait their turn.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. I cannot hear the hon. member.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I hope, Mr. Speaker, that those who are making these interjections will not acquire the kind of reputation which some members in the past have acquired, to the effect that every time they open their mouths they illustrate the emptiness of their minds.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Here is what I said on the influence of the recession on the decline of the economic activity:
During the second halt of 1957 trouble really began to spread. Demand for our products, both here and abroad, lessened. This brought excess capacity, declining private investment opportunities and, with an expanding labour force, growing unemployment. For a country like Canada, when both private investment and exports go down, you can expect a substantial increase in unemployment.

That was a consequence, or a part of it, of the recession in this country as it existed at the beginning of the election campaign. It was not very long afterwards that my analysis was confirmed by the annual report of the governor of the Bank of Canada published on February 28, 1958 and hon. members will recall the reaction of the Tory party to that statement of the governor of the Bank of Canada. I recall, and I recall very well, the reaction of the minister himself to that analysis of the situation, but what does he say now that he is chastened and sobered by the responsibility of office?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The same thing.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Oh, well let him read what he says. I quote from his carefully prepared analysis contained in the budget speech in respect of which he had the benefit of some pretty good expert advice and assistance. He does not repeat the stupid partisan charge that tight money was the cause of the change from expansion to recession, and that therefore it was all our fault. He in fact repudiates both his own and the Prime Minister's campaign explanation of the "pause". He does not even mention tight money as a cause of economic decline, but he does have a lot to say about the decrease in world demand for Canadian raw materials and our consequent condition of oversupply and unused productive capacity.
Why, his observations on this matter in the budget speech might have been written by the governor of the Bank of Canada himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about all the references to credit restrictions, high interest rates and so on, before we came into office?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister had better read his remarks as recorded at page 1231, as follows:
As the boom lost momentum in the latter part of 1957-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That was the latter part of 1957. I would now like to quote from a later passage in the same speech, as follows:
The rate of economic growth slowed noticeably during 1957 as the forces which underlay the great surge of 1955 and 1956 spent themselves.
The great surge under the Liberal administration!

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He continued and said that this surge, this excessive pace of 1955 and 1956, was straining our resources of men and materials despite very large borrowings abroad.
The Budget-Mr. Pearson
Incidentally, I do not recall hon. members opposite who were in the house in those days complaining about the excessive pace of our progress during those years, but that surge, that pace, if you like, did represent danger, the danger of serious inflation, as the minister now admits. It was Mr. Walter Harris in his budget who emphasized that danger and took steps to meet it as a result of which steps factious and partisan men condemned him and the prejudiced echoes of that condemnation are still heard in this house.
We also remember the Prime Minister and his misleading and unworthy use of carefully selected passages from a secret report of the Department of Trade and Commerce in an attempt to show that it was not inflation but recession and unemployment which was the immediate and real danger last spring. This was referred to by the hon. member for Essex East this afternoon. The Prime Minister said we had been told all this by the experts and had ignored their advice and that this had caused all the trouble.
We now know that this was a false charge and the impropriety of the tactics used in making the charge have now been illustrated by the Prime Minister himself.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: It is a true charge which has been confirmed.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If we were to be criticized- and how bitterly we were criticized in this house and on the hustings for "hiding" that report 15 months ago, when it was not asked for-what is the Prime Minister now doing when he is hiding the report of the same body for 1958, which has been asked for.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am sorry, but I cannot allow the hon. member to proceed on that phase, because that is the subject of a motion presently before the house.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Very well, Mr. Speaker, I bow to your ruling and will leave that aspect of my remarks. But I will return for a few moments, if I may, to this very important question of inflation. What does the Minister of Finance now say about inflation? He charged us on this side with taking no interest in the danger of inflation. Believe me, this question has been very much in our minds, and not only during this debate. The minister says in his budget speech: "Inflation now remains a very real danger". This is the inflation which he said in this house only last November had been checked. If this danger still exists, and it certainly does, in July 1958, how much greater was it in the spring of 1957, so we ask ourselves what light does the minister's statement and the budgetary papers accompanying it throw on this situation and

The Budget-Mr. Pearson what is the government doing to keep this danger of inflation in check.
But when I talk about this I get back to the deficit, and I am quite sure that any observations I am going to make will result in my being accused of spreading doom and gloom, as we always are on this side when we try to state the facts as we see them. Those gentlemen opposite who accuse us of spreading gloom should recall their speeches made in 1955, and before that when we were in a very mild recession and when we were subjected to a far more bitter assault than that to which the goverment is beng subjected now; when they showed much less sense of responsibility in a far less serious situation than we are trying to show in a much more serious situation. It is in this spirit I give my analysis of the danger of inflation.
The minister has provided in his main estimates for an expenditure of $5,179 million, and in his supplementary estimates for $58 million. To this we must add an old age security fund deficit amounting to $190 million, and a further $70 million with respect to the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act, plus a C.N.R. unspecified deficit, and I think the minister will probably not quarrel with me if I put this at $55 million. All this brings the total to $5,552 million against revenues estimated at $4,660 million.
That is a deficit of $892 million, and it is a deficit which even the most conservative commentators-conservative in the small "c" sense-in this country are accepting, including the director of the tax foundation. The Minister of Finance denied that this afternoon, but here is the statement of the speech which Mr. Perry of the tax foundation made, headlined: "Predicts Deficit Near $1 Billion". This is a prophecy which has not been made by us alone but by bank presidents, economists, by the head of the tax foundation, and by others qualified to form an opinion, and it will probably prove to be somewhere near the right amount because you have to add to that figure of $892 million, civil service pay increases, payments under the Agricultural Prices Stabilization Act and new payments under the gold mining act, more money, perhaps, for the provinces and so on. Therefore we have the right to say-and we can surely say it without being accused of attacking the national interest-as is being said outside this house, that on the minister's own calculation of an increase of 2 per cent in the gross national product next year, the deficit will likely be over $1 billion.
The minister does not tell us very much about how he reached his own optimistic deficit figure, but it is based on a forecast of a gross national product of $32 billion


which is, as I have said, a 2 per cent increase, assuming there is no significant rise in prices and assuming normal crops. After what we have heard this afternoon about the situation in the west, that is a somewhat risky assumption to make. However, that is his assumption. He also leads us to believe he is basing that estimate on the 1958 investment outlook, this assumption of a 2 per cent increase.
But according to the bulletin entitled "The 1958 outlook for private and public investment" published by the Department of Trade and Commerce, present investment plans indicate that total capital expenditures, both private and public, are nearly 3 per cent lower in 1958 than in 1957. We all know, of course, the great influence that capital outlays have in determining the gross national product, and it seems to me difficult to understand how the minister can reconcile a 2 per cent increase in our gross national product with a 3 per cent decrease in total capital outlay without any price rise and with agricultural prices remaining normal.
About that I would say first, that we on this side of the house are finding it impossible to accept the optimistic conclusion of the minister, and we have evidence-and it is not selective evidence, and it is not put forward for any other purpose than an attempt to face facts in a realistic way-which justifies, I think, our caution in this regard. The most recent piece of evidence we have-and the minister must surely be acquainted with it-is the figure published by the dominion bureau of statistics on the gross national product for the first quarter of 1958. That figure is $31.7 billion which, seasonally adjusted at annual rates, shows an increase of only 0.7 per cent over the comparable adjusted figure for the last quarter of 1957.
Furthermore, that particular estimate is based on an arbitrary estimate of crop production for 1958 and ignores the fact that final product prices were slightly higher in the first quarter of 1958. There was in fact a decline in volume of production of goods and services of about one half of 1 per cent compared with the same period a year ago, and a drop in the volume of non-farm output of nearly 2 per cent.
Mr. Speaker, it is impossible for us to accept this optimistic conclusion of the minister because the evidence seems to us to point in the other direction, and if that is the case surely the minister should be taking this into consideration in the plans and policies which he must be preparing at the present time.
But even if we assume an increase of 2 per cent in gross national product in 1958, what would be the employment outlook for the current year? The hon. member for

Essex East made his projection this afternoon, and I think, without going into the details he went into, that if there is this 2 per cent increase in the gross national product and if there is the same ratio between that figure and employment which has existed over recent years, it would mean we would have an increase of about 1 per cent in employment in this country in 1958 as compared with 1957. If there is an addition to the labour force of 2.5 per cent we would have considerably more unemployment next year than last year, and the peak figure would be far too high. I am willing to leave it at that.
The implications with regard to unemployment are serious, but the implications with regard to inflation are just as serious. I do not need to tell the minister this, but his dilemma-and I mentioned this in a speech in the House of Commons on the address- is that he has at the same time to deal with the danger of recession today and the danger of inflation tomorrow.
If we take into account the real budgetary deficit and the net requirement of cash nonbudgetary transactions which comes to $775 million on the minister's own figuring and which, in a sense, is a deficit of its own, the government will have to borrow-as the minister must well know because I am sure the figures are haunting him-approximately $1.8 billion in 1958-59. In addition, nearly $2 billion will be needed to pay off maturing securities. This means that the government's borrowing program for 1958-59 will reach nearly $3.8 billion of which approximately $1 billion is due to government deficit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Do not magnify that. I think my hon. friend ought to be responsible. I gave the figures.
Mi. Pearson: These are the figures which the minister himself has used.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, they are not.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the minister tell me what the figures are?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Three billion four hundred million dollars was the total I gave, not $3.8 billion.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: All right, $3.4 billion. But if the minister were to check again I think he will find that the figures total $3.8 billion.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Not at all.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is, in the minister's own words, "a major financial operation".

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is what he said.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is what the minister called it and certainly it is a major financial operation, especially when we consider the
The Budget-Mr. Pearson very important fact not mentioned by the minister, that total savings by individuals and businesses in Canada in 1957 amounted to about $6 billion and that the new capital requirements of the private sector of the economy in 1958 will amount to about $5.7 billion.
Even if the minister receives-and again I am using his own words-"the closest co-operation between the Department of Finance, the Bank of Canada, the chartered banks and all investment institutions and dealers", which he asks for and to which he is entitled, he has indeed a major financial operation ahead of him. I do not need to tell him that unskilful handling of this financial operation will have very serious consequences for the country and I am sure everyone on this side of the house will wish him well in the conduct of this complex, difficult and important operation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Thank you.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He is equal to it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If you think my predictions on these matters, coming from a political source, are suspect, I can refer again to the director of the Canadian Tax Foundation who is an accepted authority in this field. He recently stated his view that in addition to the economic deficit this year there would almost certainly be another substantial deficit in 1959 and that only a "roaring inflation"-that is what he called it although I certainly hope it can be avoided -could increase federal revenues sufficiently in the next year to balance the budget.
The director was gloomy about the long term prospects. The best he could see was a "modest federal surplus by 1967", the year that will mark the centenary of confederation. I hope that the words once applied to Sir Robert Peel when he was chancellor of the exchequer-I think by Disraeli-will not be applicable to my hon. friend. Disraeli said:
I see the chancellor of the exchequer sitting on the edge of bottomless deficits fishing for budgets.
But, says the minister, notwithstanding all these expenditures and deficits-and these are his words-the "net burden of the public debt will remain well below what we carried quite easily only a few years ago." He did not go on to say that, if this is true, it is due largely to Liberal fiscal and monetary policy after world war II. We know what that policy was. It was laid down in the white paper on unemployment and income published in 1945. That economic and financial policy was systematically and intelligently applied by Liberal governments throughout the post-war period. There were short recessions in 1949

The Budget-Mr. Ricard and 1954 and tax cuts made on those occasions helped the country get out of them. For the other years during that period inflationary pressures were predominant and there were budgetary surpluses. As a result of this anti-cyclical policy, a high and stable level of employment and income was maintained and the public debt was reduced by $2.2 billion. As the Financial Post said just the other day:
The Conservative government is thus reaping the reward of those big budget surpluses by which Mr. Abbott reduced our national debt from 1947 on by . . . $2.2 billion.
I was going to go on to talk about trade matters but I have not time for that and in any event I will have another opportunity to talk about trade. But I want to summarize by saying that this budget contains very little which gives any encouragement to us to believe that the government is going to follow an expansionist trade policy. There are indications in it-and we were not entirely reassured by the eloquence of my hon. friend the Minister of National Revenue this evening-that the government on the other hand may in a time of recession fall back on restrictionist policies which they attempted to follow with such bad results for the country in the past. There are indications in the budget, also in the field of trade, that the government is adopting a very peculiar way of preparing for the commonwealth economic conference, first by ignoring the offer of freer trade and secondly by flouting the goodwill of the British by raising the duty on woollens.
My main criticism of the budget is that it contains nothing that will effectively meet the most major domestic problem before us today, that of unemployment. There is nothing in it to encourage trade expansion. It contains very little to give us encouragement in facing the problems of unemployment and recession which lie ahead. In short, Mr. Speaker, this budget, introduced by the longest budget speech in our days, is the shortest in constructive purpose and forward-looking policy we have had since 1935. It represents an inadequate and ill-planned attack on a situation more serious than any we have faced for many years. It shows all the evidence of having been bedevilled at birth by the electoral necessities of those who produced it. There is no route here in the unplanned path that will lead us out of our difficulties. No wonder that in the country it has been received-shall I say-with indifference. That is probably the best one can say for it. It has been unwept, unhonoured and unsung. It is, in short, unworthy of the seriousness of our time.

The Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees), who is not in his seat, made an interesting comment to his constituents in Toronto on March 1 last in explaining why a budget was not brought down last autumn. The congenial minister put it this way, and I quote from the press report of his speech on that occasion:
You don't really accomplish anything in bringing down a budget.
Mr. Pallet!: That is taken completely out of context.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The budget that was brought down a few short days ago may, I am afraid, prove that the Minister of Transport was right at least on this occasion. This budget will not indeed accomplish the purpose which we all desire on all sides of the house to see accomplished, that of putting Canada back on the high road to prosperity and full employment which characterized those ten great years in our history, 1947-57. The minister should talk to his colleagues about it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since I have only a very short time at my disposal I must admit that I am confused in knowing where to start in the speech I had taken a brief moment to prepare but in view of the fact that again tonight hon. members of the Conservative party have been challenged to produce evidence concerning extravagance and waste under the previous Liberal government I would like to draw to the attention of hon. members of the Liberal party an article which appeared in the Montreal Star of January 16, 1958, which bore the following headline, "Project Launched, Then Abandoned-Cost: $6 Million". Part way through the article we find these words:
The works department paid an architect $48,675 for professional services in October, 1956, although the architect had died the previous July. The money was subsequently paid to the architect's firm but no release was obtained from the deceased's estate.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I'll bet he voted, too.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Again we read:
A foreign service officer in the external affairs department was granted 18 weeks' sick leave with pay though he had resigned from government service. Mr. Sellar said: "It is generally accepted that (sick) leave may be granted only when it may reasonably be regarded that the civil servant will return to duty upon recovery."
I ask hon. gentlemen to my right, if this is not extravagance and waste, what is it? Further along in the same article we read:
An employee of the agriculture department was paid between $1,259 and $1,659 annually for four years but $600 of the annual payment was classed as casual earnings so that the employee could qualify for war veterans allowances.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order.

speechtext: Order. It being 9.45 o'clock p.m., it is my duty, pursuant to section 6 of standing order 58, to interrupt these proceedings and put forthwith the question on the main motion.
The house in committee of ways and means, Mr. Rea in the chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
The house in
committee of ways and means to consider a proposed resolution to amend the Income Tax Act. Shall I rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again at the next sitting of the house?

Agreed.
Progress reported.
I think the leader of the house has indicated the business for tomorrow. Can he indicate the business for Monday?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Tomorrow, Mr. Speaker, we shall take the estimates of public works and agriculture. On Monday we will move to go into supply.

It being five minutes after ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
